newsitem.title: GERMANY: Harvest sunshine bodes well for German grain crop.
newsitem.headline: Harvest sunshine bodes well for German grain crop.

text.p: Hot and dry weather during the German grain harvest means farmers can bring in large volumes on time and avoid moisture problems, sources across the country said on Thursday.
Producers, who were faced with a harsh winter, drought in spring and excessive rainfall in July, are now increasingly confident of securing a large harvest.
But the lucky streak may come too late to offset some of the yield and quality reductions in wheat and rye caused by unfavourable weather earlier this year.
"It'll stay sunny and warm for at least another seven days, with temperatures between 24 and 28 degrees," a crop expert at the meteorological office DWD in Offenbach said.
"Rainfall will only be sporadic and the grain harvest can continue without any problems."
Much barley, rye, rapeseed, triticale and oats has been cut and wheat harvesting is now in full swing.
Maize and sugar beet crops will be harvested later.
Forecasts for the 1997 grain crop are above last year's 42.1 million tonnes and range up to 43 million tonnes from a four percent higher area of 7.02 million hectares.
Following is a region-by-region update --
NORTHERN GERMANY
Lower Saxony farmers were making swift harvest progress, an official at the agriculture chamber in Hanover said.
Lower Saxony, together with Bavaria in the south, is the leading grain producer.
Wheat yields could be between 6.00 and 9.00 tonnes per hectare (tph) from a wide spread of light and heavy soils.
This compared with yield expectations of 7.00-10.00 tph forecast in the most northerly state of Schleswig-Holstein with its fertile soils and Mecklenburg's 6.7 tph.
Winter wheat areas were up 10 percent at 360,000 ha, rye up at 170,000 ha (previous 160,000 ha) and barley steady at 220,000 ha.
Wheat yields looked promising but protein content could be lower than expected after heavy rain in July caused some damage.
This also depressed rye falling numbers, an indicator of baking qualities, which varied wildly.
Malting barley qualities should be fine.
WESTERN GERMANY
The Rhineland chamber of agriculture reported rye and wheat harvests were making good progress after barley harvests were delayed by two weeks in July.
Barley yields were above average -- last year's German national average was 5.61 tph -- while rye yields were positive but qualities problematic.
Millers and bakers were disappointed with protein content indications of around 11.5-12 percent in the wheat crop, which will take another few days to be completed.
Yields were mixed but Hagberg falling numbers sufficient.
The national winter wheat yield last year was 7.32 tph.
Spring crops including malting barley were showing high yields in the Rhineland.
Elsewhere in the west, wheat proteins were described as just adequate and falling numbers as satisfactory.
But two-thirds of the rye crop in North-Rhine Westphalia failed to achieve the 120 seconds falling number qualifying the grain for breadmaking.
Milling industry buyers are negotiating discounts for 100-120 seconds, but will reject any rye below 100.
SOUTHERN GERMANY
Early Bavarian wheat yields are put at around 6.5 tph but there are no reports of top yields, traders said.
Qualities appeared adequate in terms of falling numbers but protein contents could be lower than last year's due to heavy rainfall and relatively low temperatures last month.
Rye yields could be below those in 1996, but falling numbers were mostly above 120.
Spring barley, triticale and oats results were mixed.
EASTERN GERMANY
Wheat yields in the five eastern states were satisfactory while qualities and protein content were mixed, traders said.
Low protein was recorded in regions where heavy rainfall had washed away fertiliser.
But standard bread wheat qualities of the "B" variety showed good protein content and premium wheat of 15-16 percent was also being harvested.
